title: Year two close: the porch
hookLine: the school of the porch is yours to visit any time

lines: A ROOF, BUT NO FRONT WALL.
cards: A porch is a strange kind of room. It has a roof, so you can shelter there. It has no front wall, so the street comes right up to it.
People stop on the steps to talk, to wait out the rain, to watch the evening come in. Nobody checks a ticket. You can stay an hour or a minute, and come back whenever you like.
A school of philosophy started on exactly that kind of porch, and this whole year has been spent sitting on it. Today, year two closes.

teach.b: First, what a porch asks of you. Zeno taught in the open, at the painted porch in Athens. Notice what that means.
Nobody enrolls on a porch. You step up from the street, and you can step down again. Second, how the Handbook sends you off.

teach.h: HOW LONG WILL YOU PUT IT OFF?
teach.b: Near its end, Epictetus turns to his student and asks: how long will you put it off? You are not a boy any more. The contest is now; it can't be postponed.

Then he points to Socrates, who became who he was by attending to reason in everything, and says: you are not yet a Socrates, but you can live as someone who wants to be one. The book doesn't end with a diploma.
It ends by pointing at today. Third, not finished, and that's fine. Nobody leaves a year of reading as a sage.
Epictetus asked his students to show him even one Stoic and implied he'd never seen one; Seneca said plainly that he wasn't wise.
What the porch offers instead is a direction: wanting to be the kind of person Socrates was, and taking the next step on an ordinary day. Fourth, the porch stays open.

teach.h: A PORCH HAS NO DOOR TO LOCK.
teach.b: A porch has no door to lock behind you.
Whatever you kept from this year, a morning intention, an evening question, a delayed reply, you can step back up onto it any day you want. Tomorrow, year three: six questions.

how: Some people who study the Stoics keep returning to a handful of texts, the Handbook, Seneca's letters and the Meditations, rereading them over the years as guides rather than rulebooks.

o: the student who wrote down Epictetus's teaching
Epictetus's model: not yet him, but wanting to be
the founder who first taught on the painted porch

games.q: year two, from the porch — tap the pairs.
p: live as one who wants to be him

s: the Stoics are named after a porch
Zeno taught at the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch, in Athens.
near its end, the Handbook tells students to wait until they're ready
Epictetus says the contest is now and can't be put off.
Epictetus told his student he must already be a Socrates
not yet a Socrates, he says, but live as someone who wants to be one.

games.q: you're Epictetus's student, and the lessons are ending. you say: I'll start properly once I'm ready. what does he answer?
o: take all the time you need
how long will you put it off? the contest is now
games.why: Handbook 51: you are no longer a boy; the contest is here and can't be postponed. live now as someone who wants to be a Socrates.

practice: Find a step if you can, a porch, a stoop, a stair in your building, or sit in a doorway, half in and half out.
Feel the roof or the sky above you and the open side in front, and let the year come as one picture: whichever teacher, line or moment stayed.
Don't sort it or grade it; just sit with it, the way people sit on steps at the end of a day.

wordCard.voice: Socrates, the model Epictetus points to at the Handbook's end: not yet him, but someone who wants to be. Today's word, and the last of year two.

carryVoice: Your line: the porch stays open. A year closes; the steps are still there. Day six hundred ninety-six, and year two, done.

sources.work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
